newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli army readies for Hebron pullback.
newsitem.headline: Israeli army readies for Hebron pullback.

text.p: Soldiers dismantled bases and checkpoints in Hebron on Thursday awaiting approval from Israel's parliament to end 30 years of rule and transfer authority to Palestinians.
Only a handful of Palestinians watched in stinging rain as one soldier pulled down a blue-and-white Star of David flag from a sentry box at the entrance to the West Bank city.
Israeli security sources said there would be little equipment left to take away once the green light to evacuate 80 percent of the city was given.

"We are not leaving Hebron, we are redeploying in Hebron," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told parliament in Jerusalem. His remarks were aimed at right-wingers and Jewish settlers who staged a cabinet revolt against the accord sealed on Wednesday with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
The 120-member house, with Labour and left-wing opposition support, was expected to approve the U.S.-brokered agreement later on Thursday.
Netanyahu pushed the accord through cabinet by an 11-7 majority after a stormy 12-hour meeting that ended on Thursday morning.
Security sources said the army could redeploy as soon as parliament voted.

Paratroops in red berets fanned out through Hebron to cover those removing equipment and prevent protests by Jewish settlers against the agreement. Other soldiers and police set up makeshift roadblocks.
Palestinian officials said 400 civilian and paramilitary police were poised to take over.
"As soon as the redeployment begins, our forces are ready to enter the city," Hebron commander Brigadier-General Abdel-Fattah al-Jaidi told Reuters.
Palestinian police have been discreetly bringing vehicles and equipment into Hebron for months with Israel's knowledge.
Israeli cranes plucked steel sentry boxes from rooftops and rain-drenched conscripts dragged away the paraphernalia of an occupation that began before they were born.
They split open sand bags, pulled down barbed wire and dismantled search lights. A washstand too big to pass through a door was poked through one barrack-room window.
"We're very happy to see them go," said Hamed Khalil Amr, watching from his butcher shop. "We hope the settlers will do the same thing and leave our town and let us live in peace."

Some 400 militant settlers live in the heart of Hebron. Another 5,000 live in fenced enclaves on the edge of this city of 100,000 Palestinians that contains the tomb of the biblical Abraham, a site revered by Jews and Moslems.
Hebron will likely remain a flashpoint for Israeli-Arab violence even after redeployment, which is in effect, a partitioning of the city centre.
"It's a sad day when a Jewish government takes this very grave decision," settler Moshe Ben-Zimra said.
Netanyahu, addressing the settlers in parliament said: "I want to tell you, brothers and sisters, that we care about you, we don't see you as a worthless aftergrowth."

The cabinet revolt reflected the deep split in the Likud-led coalition over ceding land to Palestinians that many Israelis believe to be theirs by biblical right. Science Minister Binyamin Begin, son of the late prime minister Menachem Begin, resigned over the agreement.
